title: Amos 7:1–9
context: Amos reports three visions the Lord GOD showed him. In the first, locusts devour the latter growth after the king’s harvest; Amos pleads, Lord GOD, forgive, and the LORD relents. In the second, a judgment by fire dries up the great deep; Amos pleads again, and again the LORD relents. In the third, the Lord stands by a wall with a plumb line and declares that he will set a plumb line among his people and will not again pass by them, so the high places and sanctuaries will be laid waste and the house of Jeroboam will meet the sword. Both traditions read the visions as showing the LORD’s patience, the real place of intercession, and the seriousness of judgment. The existing boxes at 1 Samuel 15:29, Jonah 3:10, and Judges 10:16 treat how the traditions read the LORD’s relenting, the Joshua 10:14 box treats prayer and God’s purpose, and the Judges 9:23 box treats the LORD bringing disaster through created means. Jeroboam is usually taken to be Jeroboam son of Joash (Amos 1:1; 2 Kings 14:23–25).

verses.text: Thus the Lord GOD showed me: behold, he formed locusts in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and behold, it was the latter growth after the king’s harvest.
verses.arminianNotes: Thus the Lord GOD showed me: Arminian readers note that the visions begin with what the Lord GOD shows Amos; the prophet does not invent the threat but sees what is coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the locusts are formed by the Lord GOD himself, appearing after the king’s harvest. Shared ground: the vision is what the LORD shows, not a threat Amos invents.

verses.text: When they finished eating the grass of the land, then I said, “Lord GOD, forgive, I beg you! How could Jacob stand? For he is small.”
verses.arminianNotes: When they finished eating the grass of the land, then I said, Arminian readers see Amos interceding for Jacob, pleading for forgiveness because the nation is small and cannot stand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the plea, “Lord GOD, forgive, I beg you!” rests on mercy rather than merit. Shared ground: Amos intercedes for a people too small to stand.

verses.text: The LORD relented concerning this. “It shall not be,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD relented concerning this. Arminian readers see the LORD genuinely responding to Amos’s prayer by withholding the judgment he had shown, as the Jonah 3:10 box describes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the relenting as the outworking in time of God’s unchanging purpose, which includes the prayer as its means. The 1 Samuel 15:29 box sets out both readings of such language.

verses.text: Thus the Lord GOD showed me: behold, the Lord GOD called for judgment by fire; and it dried up the great deep, and would have devoured the land.
verses.arminianNotes: behold, the Lord GOD called for judgment by fire; Arminian readers see a second, more severe threat, a fire so great that it dried up the great deep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the fire would have devoured the land. The vision escalates from locusts to fire, showing the growing seriousness of the judgment Israel faces.

verses.text: Then I said, “Lord GOD, stop, I beg you! How could Jacob stand? For he is small.”
verses.arminianNotes: Lord GOD, stop, I beg you! Arminian readers see Amos interceding a second time, now asking the LORD to stop, again on the ground that Jacob is small.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the second plea asks not for forgiveness but for the judgment to cease. Both traditions see Amos as a true intercessor standing between the LORD and the people.

verses.text: The LORD relented concerning this. “This also shall not be,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “This also shall not be.” Arminian readers find in the LORD’s second relenting further evidence of his responsiveness, a mercy that the Judges 10:16 box also discusses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers again read the relenting as God’s merciful dealing in time, consistent with his unchanging character. Shared ground: both affirm the LORD’s patience and the value of intercession.

verses.text: Thus he showed me: behold, the Lord stood beside a wall made by a plumb line, with a plumb line in his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Thus he showed me: behold, the Lord stood beside a wall made by a plumb line, Arminian readers see a turn in the visions: the Lord holds a tool for testing whether a wall is straight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a plumb line measures what is already built. The image suggests that Israel is now being tested against the LORD’s standard rather than spared.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Amos, what do you see?” I said, “A plumb line.” Then the Lord said, “Behold, I will set a plumb line in the middle of my people Israel. I will not again pass by them any more.
verses.arminianNotes: I will set a plumb line in the middle of my people Israel. Arminian readers see the end of the intercession: I will not again pass by them any more, so Amos no longer pleads.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the dialogue, Amos, what do you see? leads to a decision already reached. Both traditions read the line as the close of the time of sparing.

verses.text: The high places of Isaac will be desolate, the sanctuaries of Israel will be laid waste; and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”
verses.arminianNotes: The high places of Isaac will be desolate, Arminian readers see the judgment falling on Israel’s places of worship and on the royal house, which had led the people in false worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the house of Jeroboam ended when Zechariah son of Jeroboam was killed (2 Kings 15:8-10). The text names the sword without saying how the prophecy would be fulfilled.
